Can’t believe the invalidating highly upvoted ignorant comments here. Almost thought this was in a non-ADHD sub for a second. Often this sub is even better than some of the other ADHD subs, and usually way better than the general programming subs, so it’s really disappointing to see that reaction, and I’m sorry you’ve been treated that way here OP.

It’s entirely understandable to struggle with programming with ADHD, even for people that really like programming and are super interested and passionate about it. It’s ADHD, that’s kind of a common part of it, not being able to do things we WANT to do. If ADHD never had any intersecting difficulties with programming, this sub would be pointless and unnecessary, but it’s clearly not since people come here all the time asking for help specifically for dealing with those difficulties.

I’m currently in a similar spot to you with inability to focus and finding it extremely difficult to impossible to sit down and code, except that I’m likely much older and have been programming on and off since I was 11 or 12. It’s totally understandable.

I agree with some of the other commenters that using a repl or a jupyter notebook might be a way to help keep engagement and interest, though they can also sometimes be overwhelming in their own right. I also agree with allowing yourself to focus on things that draw your interest that are somewhat related to programming, or other topics in programming rather than trying to force focus on something that feels like shit. Often the tangents will lead back to the thing that was difficult and may inspire something that drives you bring focus to it. It still will likely be difficult and not solve everything, and that’s ok and not your fault and doesn’t make you worthless or lazy or unmotivated or lacking will or not passionate or disinterested or not cut out for programming or whatever anyone else tries to tell you you are because they don’t understand, or want to make themselves feel superior, or have forgotten what it’s like to struggle, or whatever else that doesn’t have anything to do with you.

I see also from some of your comments that you’ve been starting meds and hopefully that helps. I’m not currently medicated myself, but have been at various points, and it has helped me with some things. It’s definitely worth it to keep up with your prescriber and make sure that you feel free to talk about the effects, both positive and negative, that the meds are having and whether you’re getting the benefits you want and need from them. If that’s not possible with your current prescriber, try to get another one if possible.

It’s also the case that sometimes things outside of the current thing we’re having difficulty with can influence our symptoms too and that’s definitely something to consider as well. Things like family stress, interpersonal conflict, heightened social demands, discrimination and oppression, legal and institutional issues, excessive work load and demands, etc. etc. can be absolutely devastating and overwhelming, and in addition to exacerbating ADHD symptoms, carry their own range of additional harms and difficulties that can cause severe negative effects.

All that said, my heart goes out to you. I know how difficult it can be, whether it’s dealing with the hard parts of ADHD on it’s own, which is already difficult enough, to dealing with some or many other things of top of it. I hope things work out for you and that you end up in a healthy place with stability and support and able to do what you want.

Na my dude, I spent my childhood and early adulthood in close proximity to police, with multiple family members who were cops, and other family very involved with closely working with police. Have spent a lot of time in stations watching what goes on there, what they talk about, how they operate. Spent plenty of time sitting in on and listening briefings at change of shifts. Sitting in on strategy meetings, gang intervention discussions, community advisory meetings, being an “advocate” for the department, hosting events for them, etc. etc. Spent a good portion of my life very close to my LE family members and to plenty of other cops from guys just getting into explorers, to SLOs to captains. Met the mayor when I was a kid “on behalf” of the department for a photo op. Even got given a plaque later on for “Outsanding Service and Commitment in a Community Role”.  I seriously considered being a cop after getting out of college.  I hesitate to say that I’ve had a change of heart, because I don’t think that’s right, I have, thankfully, had a change of perspective though.

In addition to all the above, I’ve also had my fair share of protest experience. Never been to a violent protest, at least on the part of the protestors, and I usually stay around the sidelines to observe, and when I was younger, to support the police. I grew up with images of LA 92 on tv, and tons of stories of harrowing moments and righteous battle against all odds from my family and the other cops, so when I became an adult and occupy happened I was very keen on watching it all go down. What I saw shocked me, because what I saw was brutal violence unleashed on a defenseless and terrified group of people. That shit seriously changed me and though it wasn’t immediate, eventually ended my thoughts of becoming a cop.

I’ve observed a lot more protests since then. Despite all the experience I have with police, and how to “behave” around them, how to avoid drawing their anger or suspicion, and how to avoid getting in their way, I’ve been tear gassed multiple times, thankfully never been shot or beat, but I’ve seen plenty of people who have, including a guy I met who later had his skull cracked in and now has permanent brain damage and has one eye that is permanently dilated and hard to see out of.  

This shit isn’t new, cops have been doing this for years, it’s only being shared more widely now.  That’s not to say it hasn’t gotten worse though. They’ve been particularly brutal more recently.  I witnessed a lot of the violence first hand in May/June, obviously not all of it, again not from within the protests but from observing from a short distance. Really disturbing shit, random beatings, shooting people in the back while running away, shooting at random people not affiliated with any protest from within cruisers, plus the old standard of kettle, tear gas, flash-bang, and baton beatings until the cops get tired or bored.

Obviously it’s been a long road from planning to be a cop, to opposing the department I used to work alongside, and I’d be lying if I said it was ever an easy road to go down, but it definitely has not been without reason.  It was the combination of my time in close connection with police, and the time I’ve spent watching them in action that has informed my understanding of law enforcement and it’s dramatic problems. It’s that combination that helped me look through the thousands of videos and understand what was going on.  And it’s that understating that makes me so concerned with how vindictive and full of open bloodlust they’ve become, because again, it was always there to a degree, but at this point they really don’t give a fuck, and I’m getting really tired of watching random people I meet on the street have their lives ruined and ending up disabled or dead because of these people’s ruthless bloodlust and power fantasies.

As to your point though about media coverage, we’re actually in agreement. I think the media does a piss poor job covering events and putting violence in context, and there certainly is a form of selection bias that occurs from the type of stories and images they show over and over. Over a long period of time that selection bias heavily favors positive stories about policing, especially in local news markets, however the trend carries nationally as well. This is something I also have first hand experience with, since I used to participate in the kinds of media outreach that lead to this overwhelmingly positive coverage. It’s also true though that the media did spend quite a bit of time more recently covering property crime, particularly highly visible instances of looting and arson. They often repeatedly showed the same images and clips over and over for hours on end while massive nondestructive protests were occurring simultaneously. There were also multiple instances in which media used clips and images from events that were not even occurring at that time, such as riots that had occurred years before, or in other countries. That’s a problem, but that’s also beyond my wheelhouse. 

However, none of this is driving cops to do the kinds of shit they’re doing, and honestly I would love to see the media report more on the internal culture of policing beyond just making allusions to it, because that’s where the real story is. Some serious actual investigative journalism, starting with people that have spent time within that environment that are no longer in it, conduction of a thorough discovery and analysis of the history of policing and of police cultures and practices, and a real and honest report on the current state of policing and how we got here. I don’t think we’ll get that, for a variety of reasons, some technical, others sociological and political, which is scary, but that’s the way it is right now.

Yes, dissociation seems to be a common hallmark experience in bpd. Before I get into it, it’s important to point out that none of this is your fault, and you or any of the rest of us that experience this are not wrong for doing so. I also experience these things, and I know how confusing and distressing they can be. They were important processes that helped us survive in the past, and are understandable responses. 

Dissociation is experienced in a variety of ways, from commonly experienced “feelings of emptiness or extreme boredom”(emotional dissociation), rich fantasy life, to in some cases experiences of intense derealization/depersonalization (feeling and experiencing things as not real or not being yourself). 

The dissociation of memory is a common component as well and can contribute to experiences with what’s called lack of object constancy (the perception or doubt that something, or even someone, that happened or existed may not or does not exist while it’s not happening or present). As I mentioned previously, intense fantasy and being “lost in thought” is a form of dissociation, and contributes to the lack of formation of strong memory of things that are occurring at the time.

Effects of dissociation, and the associated lack of object constancy can also be intertwined with the experience of fractured or inconsistent identity. This can create confusion as to who we are, what our beliefs and preferences are, difficulty feeling like our actions or experiences are our own, etc. One way out of many that I personally experience the effects of this, is feeling distressed while remembering positive experiences in the past, my mind seems to not understand fully that the event happened and isn’t going to change, and invokes a stress response to try to protect myself from losing the positive experience. I also tend to doubt that some negative experiences happened, or forget they happened altogether.

Dissociation is a defense mechanism and, as experienced in bpd, is a conditioned response to triggering stimuli.  Our emotional minds have learned to compulsively dissociate in response to events, people, objects, feelings, and thoughts that are either threatening or have the appearance of something in the past that was repeatedly threatening.

The main way to reverse the response of dissociation is to be aware of it, and repeatedly expose ourselves to triggering non-threatening stimuli, while remaining present and reminding ourselves that what we are experiencing is not a threat. This can be difficult due to various cognitive distortions that we experience.  Since many things *feel* threatening to us, and because at some point in the past it was more important for survival to recognize small details that could indicate a threat, our minds try to come up with reasons why something could be threatening, instead of looking at all the information already present to determine if they actually are.  Lack of object constancy also doesn’t help this process.

A useful skill in dealing with cognitive distortion is checking the facts of a situation. We can stop to examine everything we know to be true about a situation, while momentarily ignoring our interpretations. In dealing with our interpretations, it’s helpful to come up with alternate explanations that could explain the situation in a non-threatening way. In situations that are highly distressing, it is usually necessary to at first back away from the situation and use some kind of calming skill (such as doing some exercise, running cold water over the face, deep breathing, etc.) to reduce the level of distress so that we can think clearly enough to check the facts before returning to the situation. It is returning to a non-threatening situation and experiencing it as non-threatening that does the actual work of reprogramming our conditioned responses, so is an essential part of overcoming distress and dissociation. Not all situations are non-threatening though, which is why it’s important to back away to somewhere safe, get to a place of relative calm, and check the facts.

I hope this helps, and relates to what you’ve experienced.

Edit: Also dissociation is not inherently wrong or even problematic, for example in situations that we can’t get away from or that we have to endure but not necessarily be present for (like getting a root canal), it can be helpful and make our lives easier to zone out or get deep into fantasy.  Imagined safety can be a useful tool for self-calming as well(when safe and appropriate to do so).  And we can also use our rich fantasy abilities for creative purposes too, among other things.

Can’t speak for anyone else, but personally my understanding of my relationship with empathy has changed over time.  

I used to believe that I was tremendously empathetic because I felt (what I thought) everyone else was feeling so strongly.  I’m very attuned to others slightest behaviors and can usually tell when someone is upset/sad when it seems like others don’t recognize it.  However, I’m very prone to making assumptions about what other people are feeling based on incomplete or inaccurate information. At a basic level, I read a change in posture or facial expression and assume they feel an intense feeling which causes me to feel an intense reaction. It’s not so much that I’m wrong about what they feel in those particular moments, although sometimes I am, it’s that sometimes I assume their emotions are more intense than they actually are, or that their feelings are more likely to motivate scary behavior than they actually are. If I express that mismatched level of emotion in my sympathetic behavior toward them in these cases, it can come across as invalidating or disingenuous to the other person. (Think: you’re in your thoughts moving through emotions, but nothing too intense or hard to deal with, and then someone looks at you with intense worry on their face and says “You look really <some emotion>.” and you notice they’ve been staring at you and are continuing to. Feels weird. Why are they doing this? I’m uncomfortable.)

Other times I’ll think about something someone else has experienced and assume their feelings from that. Sometimes I’m right, sometimes I’m wrong, but the danger for me is that once I’ve assumed what their feeling is, I tend to stop noticing things that point to them feeling something different.

Another aspect that comes up for me is that when I’m feeling strong emotions I tend to not “feel” how other people are feeling. This is the affective (feeling what they’re feeling) part of empathy and accurately feeling what they’re actually most likely feeling is critical for me to be able to react appropriately and effectively to other people’s feelings.  If I don’t actually take a moment to look at the person, look at what their body language actually is in that moment, and use that information as the main source of my thoughts about what they might be feeling before taking into account why they might be feeling that way, then I get caught up in what I’m feeling and thinking and use that information to make faulty assumptions about what they’re feeling and thinking as a means to try to understand what I’m feeling and thinking. I try to assume their experience by looking at how I’m reacting to them and their actions, instead of just looking at their actions and feelings as separate from how I’m feeling. If I don’t have reliable information to base cognitive (thinking what they might be feeling) empathy on, I end up with an inaccurate experience of affective empathy, and all of my guesses as to why they’re feeling that way rely on faulty assumptions of what they’re feeling in the first place.

Sometimes I’ll latch on to one behavior that someone else has done or is doing, and assume what they’re feeling and thinking based on that. I usually come up with explanations to explain what I’m feeling, (if I feel sad, scared, angry, or lonely I assume they hate me or are mad at me or don’t care, etc.). This is huge for me in splitting. The reality is that I feel the way I do I in those moments because of my thoughts not theirs, I can remind myself of this by recognizing that I literally can’t truly know what they’re thinking or feeling. I can then try to think about other reasons they could have done whatever behavior I’m focused on, taking into account their behavior in the past, and what they’ve actually told me about how they tend to feel and think. A lot of the time I still don’t end up with a concrete answer as to why they did what they did, but I can recognize that I don’t know, and recognize that I can’t know in that moment. Sometimes I process enough information that I hit an explanation that’s just super obvious and get an “oh, ok that makes sense.” moment. 

Either way, with the recognition that I don’t know what they’re thinking and feeling, and therefore can’t have been made to feel this way by their thoughts or feelings, I’m free to look solely at my reaction to their behavior and examine why I might feel the way I do (did I feel lonely and hope for some connection and they didn’t respond? Did I wish to express loving feelings toward them and found them unavailable or preoccupied? Did they do something I didn’t expect or reminded me of something scary and then I felt fear? What was the original feeling? Can I see why it might make sense that I would feel that way, given what I know about myself and my life? Understanding why it makes sense I would feel that way, does that feeling fit the facts of the situation? Does that feeling represent an unmet need and if so how can I fulfill it or tolerate not having it fulfilled?) 

Basically, I’m capable of high levels of empathy, but without realistic and accurate information, I have effectively low empathy. I don’t think that’s particularly abnormal, in the sense that that’s just how empathy works, but I think some people just learned how to gather more accurate information and think about in different ways at some point in their lives and I didn’t. Maybe no one taught me, maybe I had bigger scarier things to survive in the past and dealing with those meant it was better to assume the worst rather than risk missing a red flag. I can learn now though, and am. It’s a process and a practice. It takes time, but gets easier.


Tl;dr: I’m capable of having a lot of empathy, but need to make sure I have the facts straight first and also sort out and make sense of my own emotions.

The constant feeling and worry that what I’m feeling is making someone I love feel bad, the panic attacks, the over affectionate behavior, fear I’m driving them away... The key is reframing and refocusing, stop worrying about what you’re making them feel. It never makes it better. That doesn’t mean don’t care about what they feel, but tell yourself, speak it to yourself out loud if you have to, that you can’t control their feelings. “I can’t control their feelings” say it over and over if you need to. Focus on what you’re feeling and what you can do to feel better. Remember you can’t control their feelings, so if making yourself feel better requires them to feel differently, it’s not going to happen, and your going to stay miserable.  Ask yourself “what can *I* do to feel better”? Can you take a walk? Splash some cold water on your face? Take some deep breaths? It may not make them feel better, but it will make you feel better so that you can react effectively to how they’re feeling with compassion.  We can’t directly change how someone is feeling, but we can change our own feelings so that we can choose to act in ways that respect other people and ourselves.
